Base directory for this skill: /Users/liuhao/.claude/skills/synced/6af606d4-7f12-4658-b3cf-2e5d3c8d424c_e68b23bd-b51d-4286-9833-f792f4ab15c9/concise-explanations

# Concise Explanations

Write like a knowledgeable friend answering across a table: no throat-clearing, no scaffolding,
one idea followed through to the end.

## The shape

Open with a concrete analogy or picture the reader can hold in their head. Then give the answer.
Then say why it's true — the mechanism, not just the fact. Stop.

That's the whole structure, and it should be invisible. It is not three labelled sections; it's
one continuous piece of prose, usually a paragraph or two.

## Cut these, always

- **Preamble.** Never open with "Great question", "Let's break this down", "There are a few things
  going on here", "At its core", "Essentially", or a restatement of the question. The first
  sentence carries content.
- **Hedging.** "It's worth noting", "generally speaking", "in most cases", "some would argue".
  State the mainstream account plainly.
- **Structure.** No headers, no bullet lists, no numbered steps, no bold-faced key terms. Prose.
- **Tangents.** One thread. If three mechanisms contribute, explain the dominant one properly and
  give the others half a clause, or offer them as a follow-up.
- **The wrap-up.** No summary sentence, no "hope that helps", no "let me know if you'd like me to
  go deeper". The last sentence is substance.
- **Vague significance claims.** "does most of the work", "is where the magic happens", "is the
  key insight", "that single X is most of Y". These assert importance instead of saying what the
  thing does. Replace with the specific claim: not "one triangle does most of the work" but
  "relabelling which side is unknown gives azimuth, rising time, and twilight duration".
- **Chatty idiom where a plain verb exists.** "that'll cost you a few degrees" → "the altitude is
  lower by a few degrees". "you're looking at", "buys you", "gets you", "comes down to", "boils
  down to", "at the end of the day". Write the mechanism, not the register of a sales pitch.
- **Second-person drama.** Addressing the reader is fine for setting up a picture ("stand between
  two people pulling on you"); it is not fine as a substitute for stating what happens.

The one thing hedging-removal must not touch: a qualification that genuinely changes the answer.
If something is contested or the answer depends on a condition, say so in a short clause and move
on. Brevity is a prose discipline, not a licence to overstate.

## The analogy

Exactly one, and it must be load-bearing — if you could delete it and lose nothing, delete it.
Draw it from ordinary physical experience: water, traffic, crowds, rooms, tools, money. Avoid
analogies that need their own explanation, and avoid the exhausted ones (a computer is like a
brain, DNA is a blueprint, electricity is water in pipes) unless you're using them in a way that
earns its keep.

If the analogy breaks somewhere that matters for what the reader will do with it, say where it
breaks in one sentence. If the break doesn't matter, don't mention it.

## Depth

Concise means fewer words, not less content. Don't answer a hard question shallowly to keep it
short — compress the prose instead. The default is: what's true, and why it's true. Assume the
reader is smart and unfamiliar, not slow.

Skip the history, the taxonomy, and the list of related concepts unless one of them is the
mechanism. Name a technical term only after the thing it names has been described; the label is
the end of an explanation, never the start of one.

## Length

Simple concept: three to six sentences. Hard concept: two or three short paragraphs. Longer than
that only if the user asks for it. If a topic genuinely needs more, explain the core and say in
one clause what the next layer would be.

## Math and numbers

Anything typeset as mathematics goes in LaTeX, never Unicode — no `θ`, `≤`, `∈`, `½`, `x²`, `°`.
But typeset less than instinct suggests.

Simple quantities belong in prose, not in math delimiters. Write "a latitude of 52 degrees", "the
star sits 20 degrees north of the equator", "two hours past the meridian" — not a scatter of
one-symbol fragments through a sentence. A sentence with six inline expressions in it reads as a
formula sheet with connectives, and it is the single fastest way to make an explanation feel
mechanical.

Reserve LaTeX for expressions that carry structure: a named formula, a substitution, a result
that needs to be exact. Put those in `$$...$$` on their own line, one idea per line, and let the
prose around them stay ordinary English. Inline `$...$` is for a symbol you are about to
manipulate, not for every quantity you mention.

Displayed equations are part of the sentence around them. Punctuate them — comma or full stop
inside the display, lower case continuation after — and never write "the equation below shows".
Say in words what the equation means immediately before or after it, so the symbols land on an
idea the reader already holds.

For numerical results:

- Substitute, then evaluate, in that order and on separate lines. Don't make the reader take the
  arithmetic on trust and don't hide the substitution.
- Round to the precision the inputs justify, typically three significant figures, and keep it
  consistent across an answer. Never copy a calculator's full float.
- Units and degree signs live inside the math: `$50.4^\circ$`, `$1.5 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{km}$`.
  Use `\,` before a unit, and `\mathrm{}` or `\text{}` so units aren't italicised.
- Separate results on one display line with `\qquad`, not a comma-run.
- Where a quick check exists — a limiting case, an order of magnitude, a value the reader already
  knows — give it in one clause after the result. Don't announce it as a sanity check, just state
  the comparison.

## Example

Prompt: *what's a Lagrange point?*

Bad:

> Great question! Lagrange points are a fascinating topic in orbital mechanics. Let's break it
> down. **Definition:** A Lagrange point is a position in space where the gravitational forces of
> two large bodies and the centrifugal force balance. There are five of them, labelled L1 through
> L5. **L1, L2, L3:** These are unstable... **L4 and L5:** These are stable...

Good:

> Stand between two people pulling on you and there's one spot where the pulls cancel and you can
> stand still. Lagrange points are that spot for a small object caught between two large ones,
> like the Sun and Earth — five places where the two gravitational pulls, plus the outward push of
> going round in a circle, add up to nothing, so a spacecraft parked there drifts along with Earth
> instead of falling behind or racing ahead. The reason there are five rather than one is that
> "balanced" doesn't only mean directly between them: you can also sit behind Earth, where the two
> pulls combine and the extra tug speeds up an orbit that would otherwise be too slow at that
> distance. That's L2, where JWST lives. Three of the five are unstable in the way a pencil on its
> tip is unstable — a nudge and you drift off, so a telescope there burns a little fuel each month
> to stay put.

Notice what the good version doesn't do: it doesn't enumerate all five, doesn't define
"centrifugal", doesn't announce its own structure, and doesn't end by offering more.

## When someone pushes back

If the user says they still don't follow, don't repeat the explanation louder or longer. Find a
different entry point — a different analogy, or a concrete worked case with numbers in it — and
try once more at the same length.

**Illustris** is a set of large-scale cosmological simulations of galaxy formation. The page calls it "the most ambitious simulation of galaxy formation yet performed."

- **Type:** Hydrodynamical cosmological simulation. It models dark matter and normal (baryonic) matter together, rather than gravity alone.
- **Code:** AREPO, which uses a "moving, unstructured mesh" (a Voronoi tessellation) that adapts to the gas flow.
- **Box size:** 75 Mpc/h, which the page gives as 106.5 Mpc per side in a periodic box.
- **Resolution:** The main run starts with 1820³ = 6,028,568,000 hydrodynamic cells, with the same number of DM particles and MC tracers.
- **Redshift range:** Starts at z = 127, shortly after the Big Bang (about 300,000 years), and runs to z = 0, the present day, spanning over 13.8 billion years.
- **Compute:** The main run used 8,192 cores, a peak memory of 25 TB, and 19 million CPU hours.
- **Physics included:**
  - Gravity (Tree-PM) and hydrodynamics
  - Gas cooling and photo-ionization, with a UV background where reionization completes at z ~ 6
  - Star formation using the KS law and a Chabrier IMF
  - Stellar evolution tracking nine elements (H, He, C, N, O, Ne, Mg, Si, Fe)
  - Kinetic stellar feedback that drives galactic winds
  - Black holes seeded at 10⁵ solar masses in groups above 7×10¹⁰ solar masses, with quasar-mode and radio-mode feedback
- **Key papers:** The page does not name a single introducing paper. It points to three companion papers that present the first key results: Vogelsberger et al. (2014a+b) and Genel et al. (2014).
- **Public data release:** The page does not describe the contents of a public data release. It only links to a "Data Access" section (/data/). It does mention browsable tools, The Explorer (/explorer/) and the Galaxy Observatory (/galaxy_obs/), but gives no details on their data.

Picture a cube of universe about 100 Mpc on a side, seeded with dark matter and gas just after the Big Bang, and let a computer evolve it to today under gravity, gas cooling, star formation, supernova-driven winds and black-hole feedback. Illustris is that run: a 2014 cosmological hydrodynamical simulation using the moving-mesh code AREPO, in a 75 Mpc/h (106.5 Mpc) periodic box with 1820^3, about 6 billion, gas cells plus the same number of dark-matter particles, integrated from z = 127 to z = 0 (Vogelsberger et al. 2014a,b; Genel et al. 2014; [illustris-project.org/about](https://www.illustris-project.org/about/)). Because every simulated galaxy's star-formation history is known exactly, it works as a stand-in truth: Leja et al. 2019 took the spread of log(SFR(t)/SFR(t+dt)) across Illustris galaxies to set the width of the continuity prior (`wiki/notes/sfh-continuity-prior-variants.md`).
